title: THE_LOAD_BEARING_REPOS
description: A Thanksgiving thank-you to the maintainers whose code holds up the internet, and how to help them—featuring curl, jq, and SQLite.
content: 🗞️ issue 015: the load-bearing repos: giving thanks to the code holding up the internet it's thanksgiving week in the us, so this issue is a thank-you note to code most of us never think about. xkcd's "dependency" draws modern infrastructure balanced on one thin block that some random person in nebraska maintains, and every engineer can name their own. the 2024 xz backdoor showed the risk: an attacker spent over two years earning maintainer trust. that's no reason to blame maintainers, and a strong one to help them. so: three tools to thank, twelve more on the radar, and ways to chip in at the end. grab your coffee. open your terminal. let's start hacking. 🔬 the sandbox: 3 projects i tested this week 1. curl 🌐 (data transfer) what is it? curl is a command-line tool for moving data with urls, built on libcurl, the c library that does the actual work; its readme lists 25 protocols, from http and ftp to mqtt and sftp. the project's history page traces it to httpget 0.1, a small tool rafael sagula released in november 1996, which daniel stenberg took over and extended, and which became curl with the release of curl 4 in march 1998. it is distributed under an mit-like license, and curl's governance page defines a maintainer as a project volunteer with the right to merge changes. why you should care: when a request misbehaves, curl takes your application out of the picture: -v prints verbose transfer details, -i fetches headers only, and --resolve overrides dns for one host and port, which the manual calls an /etc/hosts alternative on the command line. the first line of curl --version names the third-party libraries linked into your build, such as the tls library and zlib, so one command shows how many other projects hold curl up. the project's bug-reporting page also says exactly what to include: your version and os, what you expected, and how to repeat the problem. my rating: handshake everywhere 4.9/5 ⭐ website: github.com/curl/curl 💻 get started: curl --version | head -n 1 && curl -si https://curl.se | head -n 1 2. jq 🔎 (json processor) what is it? jq is a command-line json processor that its homepage describes as sed for json data: you write a short filter, and it slices, maps and reshapes structured input. it is written in portable c with zero runtime dependencies, so a single binary can be copied to another machine of the same type, and it is mit-licensed. stephen dolan created it (the repository dates to 2012), and after a five-year gap between releases, a new group of maintainers moved the project to the jqlang github organization in 2023 and shipped jq 1.7. why you should care: pipe any json-speaking command into it: -r prints strings without quotes, -n runs a filter with no input at all, and $env exposes your environment variables as an object, which is all the get started line below needs. the project's own story is the second reason to care, because the 1.7 release notes open with the five-year hiatus and thank the new owners, admins and maintainers who got the long-awaited release out. that is what keeping a load-bearing tool alive looks like: new people taking on the ci, documentation and release chores. my rating: second-wind filter 4.8/5 ⭐ website: github.com/jqlang/jq 💻 get started: brew install jq && jq -nr '$env.path | split(":")[]' 3. sqlite 🗄️ (embedded database) what is it? sqlite is an in-process c library that implements a self-contained, serverless, zero-configuration, transactional sql database engine: there is no server process, and a complete database with tables, indices, triggers and views lives in a single ordinary disk file. the source code is in the public domain. one accuracy note: sqlite/sqlite on github is an official git mirror, and its readme says development happens in fossil, the version control system written to support sqlite, at sqlite.org/src. why you should care: the file format is cross-platform, so a database copies cleanly between 32-bit and 64-bit systems or between big-endian and little-endian ones, and the project says sqlite is likely used more than all other database engines combined, found in every android device, iphone, mac and windows 10/11 install and every firefox, chrome and safari browser. a team on three continents writes it, and the source files open with a blessing in place of a legal notice: "may you share freely, never taking more than you give." for bugs, use the project's forum; it does not accept patches without a public-domain affidavit, so a precise report is the practical way to help. my rating: single-file bedrock 4.9/5 ⭐ website: github.com/sqlite/sqlite 💻 get started: sqlite3 ttt.db "create table t(x);" && ls -l ttt.db ☕ the curious non-dev: no code required why does so much of the internet depend on a handful of volunteers? think of the pipes inside a city's walls. nobody designs a new fitting for every house; everyone buys the standard one because it connects to everything else. software works the same way for solved problems like compressing a file, reading a time zone or opening a secure connection: one good library gets reused everywhere, and open-source licenses let anyone do that without paying or asking. a 2024 harvard business school working paper put the supply-side value of widely used open source (the cost of building it once) at $4.15 billion, the demand-side value (what every company using it would pay to replace it) at $8.8 trillion, and found that over 95% of that demand-side value comes from about 5% of developers. who are those developers? in tidelift's 2024 survey, 60% of the more than 400 maintainers who answered called themselves unpaid hobbyists, and only 12% earned most or all of their income from maintenance. funding does exist: sqlite has a consortium of member companies, and in 2026 the city of munich began paying libexpat's maintainer for up to six months. but think of the plumbing again. a water utility meters every household and sends a bill; nothing meters a library, so no bill goes out. that mismatch, not carelessness or villainy, is how load-bearing code ends up resting on a handful of people. 📡 the radar: 12 more load-bearing repos to thank this weekend 🧱 foundations under everything 1. madler/zlib (~7.2k stars) - jean-loup gailly and mark adler's compression library, copyrighted since 1995, implements the zlib, deflate and gzip formats, and its readme still asks volunteers to write the man pages. 2. openssl/openssl (~31.1k stars) - a toolkit for tls, dtls and quic plus a general-purpose crypto library, descended from eric young and tim hudson's ssleay and licensed under apache 2.0. 3. libexpat/libexpat (~1.4k stars) - a c99 streaming xml parser started by james clark in 1997 under an mit-style license; in 2026 the city of munich began funding its maintainer for up to six months. 4. tukaani-project/xz (~1.7k stars) - xz utils, the liblzma library and xz tool, whose lzma2 compression the project says makes typical files about 30% smaller than gzip; its 5.6.0 and 5.6.1 tarballs carried the 2024 backdoor. 🕰️ time, text & pixels 5. eggert/tz (~1.9k stars) - the mostly public-domain time zone database behind python's zoneinfo, updated as governments change their clocks, sometimes with little warning, with patches sent by email to tz@iana.org rather than github. 6. pcre2project/pcre2 (~1.4k stars) - a bsd-licensed c library for perl-compatible regular expressions with an optional jit engine, which the project says is bundled in products from excel and safari to apache and git. 7. harfbuzz/harfbuzz (~6.2k stars) - the text shaping engine the project says shapes the majority of text on modern screens, named from persian harf (letter) and buzz (open) as a calque of opentype. 8. imagemagick/imagemagick (~17.8k stars) - the image conversion suite that the title text of xkcd 2347 jokes will one day break for good; its readme urges you to write a security policy for your environment before using it. 🔧 quiet workhorses 9. libuv/libuv (~27.3k stars) - an mit-licensed asynchronous i/o library built primarily for node.js and also used by julia, luvit and uvloop, with one event loop over epoll, kqueue, iocp and event ports. 10. rsyncproject/rsync (~5.3k stars) - the file copier that sends just the differences between files across the link, shipped with the technical report describing its delta-transfer algorithm. 11. tmux/tmux (~50.0k stars) - an isc-licensed terminal multiplexer whose sessions keep running after you detach, built for openbsd, freebsd, netbsd, linux, macos and solaris; its readme says bug reports and especially code contributions are most welcome. 12. git/git (~64.1k stars) - originally written by linus torvalds and developed on its mailing list, not github; this repo is a publish-only mirror, and gitgitgadget turns pull requests into list patches. 🏗️ closing thoughts what stands out in this list is how plain the work is: munich paying for six months of libexpat upkeep, jq's new team shipping a release after five quiet years, zlib's readme still asking someone to write man pages, tz's contributors emailing rule changes with sources. nothing heroic, just sustained attention. the xz incident is the reminder that trust is a security control too, since a stranger spent two years earning it. more helping hands, not more blame, is the fix. here is the short list. pay: curl takes donations through open collective, git takes them through the software freedom conservancy, imagemagick takes github sponsors, and companies can fund sqlite through its consortium. report well: curl ended its bug bounty in january 2026, citing a surge of ai-generated slop reports and a confirmed-vulnerability rate below one in twenty, so a verified, reproducible report is a real gift. send fixes upstream instead of carrying a private patch, but read the rules first: git wants patches on its mailing list, tz wants plain email with sources, and sqlite wants a public-domain affidavit. which small project quietly holds up your stack, and when did you last thank its maintainers? tell me on x (twitter) or linkedin. until next thursday, keep your servers close and support your local maintainers.

title: JUST_USE_POSTGRES
description: Queues, search, vectors and REST APIs inside the database you already run, with the limits spelled out—featuring pgvector, PostgREST, and PGlite.
content: 🗞️ issue 014: just use postgres: one database to replace half your stack every feature request adds a box to the architecture diagram: redis for jobs, elasticsearch for search, a vector database for embeddings, kafka for events. each box brings its own backups, auth and 3 a.m. failures, plus a second copy of data your database already holds. meanwhile postgres extensions can run queues, search, vectors and schedulers inside the same transactions and backups as your tables. this issue is postgres first, with exit criteria, and a plain note on where kafka, elasticsearch and vector databases still win. grab your coffee. open your terminal. let's start hacking. 🔬 the sandbox: 3 projects i tested this week 1. pgvector 🧭 (vector search) what is it? pgvector is a postgres extension written in c, under the postgresql license, that adds a vector column type and distance operators such as <- for l2 and <= for cosine, on postgres 13 and newer. search is plain sql and exact by default, and an hnsw or ivfflat index trades some recall for speed. the get started line assumes a running homebrew postgresql@17 or postgresql@18, the only two the formula covers, and opens psql, where create extension vector; switches it on for that database (the readme also documents an official docker image, pgvector/pgvector). why you should care: embeddings sit next to the rows they describe, so one query can mix similarity, a where clause and a join inside one transaction, and the readme lists replication and point-in-time recovery through the write-ahead log, so no sync job has to keep a second database honest. read the limits first: approximate indexes filter after the index scan, so with the default hnsw.ef_search of 40 a filter that matches 10% of rows returns about 4 results on average (iterative scans, added in 0.8.0, address that), and indexes stop at 2,000 dimensions for vector and 4,000 for halfvec. past one machine the readme says to scale up, then add replicas or shard with citus or pgdog, and that is the point where a purpose-built vector database earns a look. my rating: vendor-free vectors 4.8/5 ⭐ website: github.com/pgvector/pgvector 💻 get started: brew install pgvector && psql postgres 2. postgrest 🔌 (database to rest api) what is it? postgrest is a web server written in haskell, under the mit license, that serves a rest api straight from an existing postgres database. you point it at a schema and it turns the tables, views and functions there into endpoints (a function is called with a post to /rpc/function_name), pushing as much work as possible into the database, including serializing the json response in sql. authentication is a jwt whose role claim makes postgrest switch to the database role of that name for the length of the request, so postgres roles and privileges, not controller code, decide who can do what. why you should care: anything in the exposed schema becomes an endpoint without a controller, a serializer or an orm model, the constraints in your schema stay the single source of truth for validation, and the openapi description it generates feeds tools like swagger ui. the docs recommend exposing views and functions instead of raw tables, so the schema you publish can change shape without breaking clients. the trade-off is that your business rules now live in sql functions, views and constraints, so a team that wants them in typescript or go is better served by a conventional app server in front of postgres. my rating: the controller-free zone 4.6/5 ⭐ website: github.com/postgrest/postgrest 💻 get started: brew install postgrest && postgrest --example 3. pglite 📦 (embedded postgres) what is it? pglite is postgres compiled to webassembly and packaged as a typescript library by electric, so it runs in node.js, bun, deno or a browser with no other dependencies, and the readme puts it at about 3 mb gzipped. the readme says there is no linux virtual machine involved, and because webassembly can't fork processes, it uses postgres' single-user mode and talks to it through an input/output pathway from javascript. databases can live in memory, on the file system or in indexeddb, extensions such as pgvector and postgis are supported, and the license is your choice of apache 2.0 or the postgresql license. why you should care: tests and local-first apps get a postgres engine in-process, started with new pglite(), so the test database stops being a different engine that disagrees with production about edge cases. the limit is in the readme: pglite is single user and single connection, which makes it a fit for tests, prototypes and apps that embed their own database, and not a stand-in for a server with a pool of clients. the readme also carries an alpha status badge, so pin your version and check the docs before you build a product on it. my rating: pocket elephant 4.7/5 ⭐ website: github.com/electric-sql/pglite 💻 get started: npm install @electric-sql/pglite ☕ the curious non-dev: no code required what is a database extension, and how can one database replace five services? think of postgres as a stand mixer. the motor does the hard, valuable work: storing data durably, making every change all-or-nothing, and recovering after a crash. an extension is an attachment that clicks onto that motor. technically, create extension runs a script that adds new building blocks to one database, such as data types, functions, operators and index support, and it records them so the whole bundle can be removed again. one attachment teaches the database to compare embeddings, another runs jobs on a schedule, another adds a message queue, and all of them borrow the same motor, the same backups and the same permissions. so how does one database replace five services? each of those services is mostly an attachment that arrived with its own motor: its own storage, crash recovery, accounts and backups. fold the attachment into the database you already run and the spare motor goes away, along with the awkward moment where two systems disagree, because a queued job and the order it refers to can be saved in one transaction or not at all. the caveat is that a few jobs need a bigger machine than any attachment. kafka spreads topics across servers and elasticsearch spreads an index across a cluster. when you need that, you stop attaching and buy the industrial mixer. 📡 the radar: 12 more boxes to delete from your diagram this weekend 🧩 extensions that replace services 1. citusdata/pg_cron (~3.9k stars) - a job scheduler that runs inside postgres as an extension: cron syntax or an interval of 1 to 59 seconds, jobs stored in a cron.job table, and a rule that two runs of the same job never overlap. 2. pgmq/pgmq (~5.4k stars) - an sqs-style message queue built from plain postgres sql objects, with no background worker, exactly-once delivery within a visibility timeout, and archiving instead of deletion when you want replay. 3. paradedb/paradedb (~9.5k stars) - the readme's own tagline is "just use postgres," and it ships a rust extension with a custom index for bm25 full-text and vector search, plus filters and aggregations; the community edition is agpl-3.0. 4. postgis/postgis (~2.3k stars) - adds gis simple features, r-tree indexing and a long list of spatial functions to postgres; this github repo is a mirror, and the project's official home is at osgeo. 🛠️ migrations & operations 5. xataio/pgroll (~6.6k stars) - a go cli for zero-downtime, reversible schema migrations that serves old and new schema versions side by side, backfills columns when needed, rolls back instantly, and works with rds and aurora. 6. pgbackrest/pgbackrest (~4.5k stars) - backup and restore for postgres, written in c and mit licensed, with parallel processing, lz4 and zstd compression, backups from a standby, multiple repositories and a custom protocol over tls or ssh. 7. ankane/pghero (~8.9k stars) - a performance dashboard for postgres that starts with one docker run and a database url, or mounts as a rails engine, with query stats built on the pg_stat_statements module. 8. dbcli/pgcli (~13.4k stars) - a postgres client in python built on prompt_toolkit, with context-sensitive auto-completion and pygments syntax highlighting; on macos it is one brew install away. ⚙️ postgres as a platform 9. riverqueue/river (~5.8k stars) - a transactional job queue on postgres or sqlite for go, typescript, ruby and rust: jobs exist if their transaction commits, vanish if it rolls back, and stay invisible to workers until commit. 10. graphile/worker (~2.4k stars) - a node.js job queue that uses listen/notify to start jobs in milliseconds, per its docs, with cron tasks at minute granularity and delayed or debounced jobs; the readme pairs it with postgrest. 11. neondatabase/neon (~23.3k stars) - an open-source serverless postgres platform written in rust that separates storage from compute: stateless postgres nodes sit on a pageserver for storage and safekeepers, a redundant wal service. 12. pgbouncer/pgbouncer (~4.4k stars) - a lightweight connection pooler written in c, with session, transaction and statement pooling modes and a documented default of about 2 kb of memory per connection. 🏗️ closing thoughts this ecosystem leans on a friendly base license. postgres says it is committed to staying free and open source and has no plans to change the postgresql license, and a permissive base lets anyone ship an extension: pgvector, pgmq and pg_cron use that license, pgbackrest is mit and pgbouncer is isc. not everything is that permissive, so read the terms before you wire something into a product, because paradedb's community edition is agpl-3.0 and postgis is gpl. every extension is also a dependency you upgrade in lockstep with postgres, so check the supported versions before a major upgrade; pgmq's readme lists postgres 14 to 18, for example. the rule to steal isn't "never add a service." it's to add one on purpose, with a number in your hand. pool connections early, watch your slow queries, and test your restores instead of trusting that backups exist. then write down the limit that would make you move a workload out: events that many consumers must replay, a search cluster, a vector index that outgrew one machine. postgres first, with an exit sign you wrote yourself. which service in your stack would you delete first if postgres could do its job, and which one is staying no matter what? tell me on x (twitter) or linkedin. until next thursday, keep your servers close and support your local maintainers.

title: THE_OBSERVABILITY_ORACLES
description: Keeping logs, metrics, and traces in-house with OpenTelemetry and open-source backends—featuring SigNoz, OpenObserve, and VictoriaMetrics.
content: 🗞️ issue 013: the observability oracles: logs, metrics and traces without the datadog bill every request your service handles leaves exhaust behind: a few log lines, a handful of spans, a nudge on a dozen counters. multiply that by every pod and every deploy, and telemetry becomes the one dataset that grows with your traffic instead of your headcount. if the meter is per gigabyte, per host or per custom metric, the incentives go sideways: somebody deletes the debug logs, somebody else drops the high-cardinality label, and the first incident that needs exactly that detail finds it gone. nobody budgets for that conversation, but it tends to land in the same thread as the invoice. this isn't a takedown of any single vendor; it's an argument about who gets to set the meter. two things changed. opentelemetry made instrumentation a vendor-neutral standard: its docs describe an open-source cncf project that works with open-source and commercial backends alike, and promise that you own the data you generate. and several open-source backends now come in shapes a small team can realistically run. signoz keeps all three signals in one clickhouse columnar database, openobserve writes parquet from a single rust binary, and victoriametrics ships as one dependency-free binary. collectors like vector and the opentelemetry collector sit in front and can transform and route data before it lands. none of this is free, because you inherit the disks, the upgrades and the pager, but at least the meter is yours. grab your coffee. open your terminal. let's start hacking. 🔬 the sandbox: 3 projects i tested this week 1. signoz 🔭 (full-stack observability) what is it? signoz is an open-source observability platform built on opentelemetry that keeps logs, metrics and traces in a single clickhouse columnar database behind one ui, so you can pivot from a slow trace to the logs and metrics around it. the self-hosted stack is five containers (clickhouse, clickhouse keeper, postgresql for metadata, an opentelemetry-based collector and the signoz server), installed with the project's foundry tool. the code is mit outside the ee/ and cmd/enterprise/ directories, which carry a separate enterprise license; the company also offers a hosted cloud and an enterprise tier. why you should care: send otlp from any opentelemetry sdk or collector to ports 4317 and 4318 and you get apm views, a log explorer, dashboards and alerts, with metrics queryable through a query builder, promql or clickhouse sql. the readme's own log benchmark claims 50% lower resource requirements than elastic during ingestion, which is the project's number, so replay it on your own logs. budget at least 4 gb of memory for docker, read the curl-to-bash installer before you run it (it drops foundryctl in ~/.local/bin, often missing from path on macos), and note that the noz ai assistant is cloud-only. my rating: full-moon oracle 4.7/5 ⭐ website: github.com/signoz/signoz 💻 get started: u=https://signoz.io/foundry.sh && curl -fssl $u | bash && foundryctl gen examples && cd docs/examples/docker/compose && foundryctl cast 2. openobserve 🔮 (single-binary observability) what is it? openobserve (o2) is a single rust binary for logs, metrics and traces that stores data as parquet files in an s3-native design and queries it with sql, plus promql for metrics. it takes opentelemetry's otlp natively, so sdks and collectors can send straight to it. the open-source edition is agpl-3.0; sso, advanced rbac, audit trails and federated search sit in a separate enterprise edition under a commercial license. why you should care: the readme claims up to 140x lower storage cost than elasticsearch, with better queries on about a quarter of the hardware; those are the project's own comparisons, so replay your own logs first. ingest-time pipelines can enrich, redact or reduce data before it's stored, and the faq says there are no shards, replicas or heap sizes to manage. the catch: ingested data is immutable and only whole retention periods can be dropped, so think twice before sending it personal data. the command below is the readme's quick start: open localhost:5080 and log in with the root account it creates, and swap that example password before anything real reaches it. my rating: parquet prophet 4.6/5 ⭐ website: github.com/openobserve/openobserve 💻 get started: e=root@example.com && p=complexpass123 && docker run -d --name openobserve -v $pwd/data:/data -p 5080:5080 -e zo_root_user_email=$e -e zo_root_user_password=$p openobserve/openobserve:latest 3. victoriametrics 📈 (time-series database) what is it? victoriametrics is a time-series database and monitoring solution written in go under the apache 2.0 license, shipped as a dependency-free single-node binary configured through command-line flags, with a cluster version that is open source too. it scrapes prometheus exporters, accepts prometheus remote write, and also ingests influxdb, graphite, opentsdb, datadog agent and opentelemetry metrics. you query it with promql or its own metricsql, in a built-in ui at localhost:8428/vmui; the homebrew service scrapes itself every 10 seconds, so there is data to look at within seconds. why you should care: point an existing prometheus at it with remote write and keep your exporters, dashboards and alert rules; the readme pitches it as long-term storage for prometheus, or a drop-in replacement for prometheus and graphite in grafana. its own benchmarks claim up to 7x less ram and 7x less storage than prometheus, thanos or cortex, a cost lever you can test in an afternoon. it covers metrics only: logs and traces have sibling projects, victorialogs and victoriatraces, and downsampling, multiple retentions and anomaly detection are enterprise features. my rating: seer of series 4.8/5 ⭐ website: github.com/victoriametrics/victoriametrics 💻 get started: brew install victoriametrics && brew services start victoriametrics ☕ the curious non-dev: no code required what is the difference between logs, metrics and traces? picture a courier company. a metric is a number on the depot wall: parcels handled per hour, average delivery time, vans currently out. opentelemetry defines it as a measurement captured at runtime, and because it's just a number, it's usually small to keep. a log is the driver's notebook, one timestamped entry per event, such as "door locked, left with neighbour". it holds the detail, but only if you know which notebook to open. a trace is the tracking page for one parcel: every hop in order, with how long it sat at each, or in opentelemetry's words, the path of a request through your application. you use them as a chain. the metric tells you something is wrong: delivery times doubled at 14:00. the trace of one slow parcel tells you where: it sat for 40 minutes at a single depot. that depot's notebook for those 40 minutes tells you why: the scanner kept crashing. tools link the three by stamping trace and span ids onto log lines, which an active opentelemetry sdk does automatically for your existing logs. it also explains where the volume comes from. metrics grow with the number of distinct series you create, while logs and traces record individual events and grow with traffic. 📡 the radar: 12 more oracles for your stack this weekend 📊 metrics & dashboards 1. prometheus/prometheus (~66.8k stars) - a cncf project that pulls metrics over http from your targets and stores them as time series defined by a metric name plus key/value dimensions; each server node is autonomous, with no distributed storage to run. 2. grafana/grafana (~77.6k stars) - the dashboard layer for metrics, logs and traces, where each query picks its own data source so one graph can mix them; licensed agpl-3.0-only, with some apache-2.0 exceptions. 3. perses/perses (~2.5k stars) - a cncf sandbox dashboard tool built around an open dashboard specification, with go and cue sdks for dashboards-as-code and data sources for prometheus, tempo, loki and pyroscope. 4. netdata/netdata (~81.2k stars) - per-second metrics with zero configuration and unsupervised ml anomaly detection; the agent is gplv3+, but the readme calls the dashboard ui closed-source, if free to use. 📜 logs, traces & pipelines 5. grafana/loki (~29.1k stars) - prometheus-style log aggregation that indexes only a set of labels per log stream, not the log text itself, which the readme says makes it simpler to operate and cheaper to run. 6. jaegertracing/jaeger (~23.3k stars) - distributed tracing created at uber and graduated at the cncf in october 2019, with an all-in-one build that bundles the ui, collector, query service and in-memory storage. 7. vectordotdev/vector (~22.8k stars) - a rust pipeline that collects, transforms and routes logs and metrics to any backend; the readme lists cutting observability costs as a use case and says datadog's open-source team maintains it. 8. open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector (~7.7k stars) - the vendor-agnostic binary that receives, processes and exports traces, metrics and logs, so you don't run a separate agent for every data format; one codebase deploys as an agent or as a collector. 🚨 uptime & alerting 9. louislam/uptime-kuma (~93.0k stars) - a self-hosted uptime monitor with a reactive ui, 20-second check intervals, status pages you can map to your own domains and 90+ notification services. 10. twin/gatus (~12.4k stars) - a developer-oriented health dashboard where yaml conditions such as a 200 status and a response time under 300 ms decide whether an endpoint is healthy, paired with alerts to slack, pagerduty and more. 11. healthchecks/healthchecks (~10.5k stars) - cron monitoring in reverse: your jobs ping it over http or email, and when a ping doesn't arrive on time it alerts you; a bsd-licensed django app that also runs as a hosted service. 12. keephq/keep (~12.5k stars) - an alert management layer that pulls alerts from your monitoring tools into one pane, with deduplication, correlation, enrichment and workflows; mit-licensed outside its ee/ directory. 🏗️ closing thoughts read the licenses before the feature lists. signoz and keep put an ee/ directory under a separate license, openobserve and victoriametrics both offer commercial enterprise editions with extra features, and netdata's readme calls its dashboard ui closed-source but free to use. none of that is a scandal, since the free parts do real work, but it tells you what you can fork if the roadmap and your needs ever part ways. the durable move sits upstream of any backend. instrument with opentelemetry, put a collector or vector in front, and decide there what gets kept, sampled or dropped. then the backend is a replaceable part, and the day a license, a price or a maintainer changes, you rewrite a config file instead of every service. running it yourself isn't free either: you take on the disks, the upgrades and the 3 a.m. page that a vendor used to absorb, so count those hours before you count the savings. which signal would you keep if you could only afford one: logs, metrics or traces? tell me on x (twitter) or linkedin. until next thursday, keep your servers close and support your local maintainers.

title: GIT_SORCERY
description: Rebasing, splitting, and untangling git history without losing your mind—featuring Jujutsu, Difftastic, and Delta.
content: 🗞️ issue 012: git sorcery: rewriting history without losing your mind most of us live in a five-command subset of git: add, commit, push, pull, and a quiet prayer. everything else gets treated like a live wire. take interactive rebase: you edit a text file of verbs like pick, squash and drop, git replays your commits one at a time, and the first conflict stops it halfway through. the safety nets are real, since git rebase --abort returns your branch to its original state and the reflog remembers where it used to point. but nobody advertises them, so the history fills up with "wip", "fix", "fix again" and "actually fix", and whoever runs git bisect six months from now pays the bill. the answer isn't to memorize more flags. git's data model is fine; its controls are the problem, and a newer generation of tools replaces the controls without touching the engine. jujutsu keeps your commits in a git repository but treats rewriting them as an everyday operation, with an undo log behind it. difftastic compares syntax trees instead of lines, so a reformat stops burying the one real edit. delta makes the diff itself readable, and git-absorb works out which commit each fix belongs to. none of them needs your teammates to switch, because what reaches the remote is still ordinary git commits. grab your coffee. open your terminal. let's start hacking. 🔬 the sandbox: 3 projects i tested this week 1. jujutsu 🥋 (version control) what is it? jujutsu (command: jj) is a version control system written in rust under the apache 2.0 license that keeps its commits and files in an ordinary git repository, so it works with any git remote and, in a colocated checkout, side by side with git itself. its model differs from git's in a few basic ways: the working copy is itself a commit that is amended automatically, there is no staging area, and every change keeps a stable id while its commit hash changes on each rewrite. martin von zweigbergk started it as a hobby project in late 2019; google is a main contributor, but the readme is explicit that it is not a supported google product. why you should care: edit a commit anywhere in your stack and every descendant is rebased automatically; conflicts get recorded in the commits instead of freezing you halfway through a rebase, so you resolve them when you choose to. every operation lands in an operation log, so jj undo takes back the last one (a botched rebase included), while jj split and jj squash -i carve and recombine commits without a todo list. try it in a throwaway clone first, since the readme still calls jujutsu experimental and the docs list git hooks as unsupported. my rating: black-belt undo 4.8/5 ⭐ website: github.com/jj-vcs/jj 💻 get started: brew install jj && jj git init && jj log 2. difftastic 🔮 (structural diff) what is it? difftastic is a diff tool written in rust under the mit license that detects the language, parses both files with tree-sitter grammars, and compares the syntax trees instead of the lines. because it compares trees, a method chain reflowed onto new lines comes out as unchanged, and the matching itself is a route-finding problem on a graph that it solves with dijkstra's algorithm. for file types it doesn't know, and for extremely large inputs, it falls back to a line-based diff with word highlighting. why you should care: formatter commits, re-indented html and reflowed call chains stop burying the one real edit in review, and a file that was only reformatted just prints "no syntactic changes." run git -c diff.external=difft diff in any repo with uncommitted changes (add --ext-diff for show and log -p), or wire it into jujutsu with a two-line diff-formatter setting. the readme is upfront about the trade-offs: the output is for humans and can't be applied as a patch, and it scales poorly on files with a large number of changes. my rating: crystal-ball diff 4.7/5 ⭐ website: github.com/wilfred/difftastic 💻 get started: brew install difftastic && git -c diff.external=difft diff 3. delta ✨ (diff pager) what is it? delta is a syntax-highlighting pager for git, diff, grep and blame output, written in rust under the mit license. git pipes its output through it, and it re-renders the diff with the same syntax themes as bat, word-level highlights inside changed lines (via a levenshtein edit-inference algorithm), optional side-by-side panes and line numbers. the package is called git-delta in most package managers, but the executable is just delta. why you should care: set core.pager = delta once and your git diff, git show, git log -p and git blame output comes out highlighted, with n and n jumping between files once navigate = true is set. its improved merge-conflict display helps mid-rebase, and code copied out of a diff arrives without the + and - markers. it also ships an emulation mode for diff-so-fancy, and jujutsu's docs show the config for using delta as its pager. my rating: syntax potion 4.6/5 ⭐ website: github.com/dandavison/delta 💻 get started: brew install git-delta && git show | delta --side-by-side ☕ the curious non-dev: no code required what actually is a commit, and how can you "rewrite history" without losing anything? a commit is a snapshot, not a list of edits. each one stores the full state of a project at one moment, plus a note, an author, a timestamp and a pointer to the commit that came before it. picture a stack of dated photographs of a whiteboard, each stapled to the one beneath it and stamped with a fingerprint computed from its own contents and the fingerprint below. a branch is just a sticky flag on one photo, and the flag is what moves when you add a new one. that chaining makes history tamper-evident: change one photo and its fingerprint changes, and so does every fingerprint stacked above it. so "rewriting history" never edits a photo in place. it reshoots from the photo you want to change upward, staples the new stack onto the old base, and moves the flag to the top of the new stack. the old stack isn't shredded: git keeps a local log of where every flag used to sit, called the reflog, and by default it holds on to old positions for at least 30 days. that's how a botched rewrite gets undone. the golden rule is to do this before you share. once colleagues hold copies of the old photos, two competing versions of the story exist, and somebody has to reconcile them. 📡 the radar: 12 more spells for your git grimoire this weekend 🪚 history surgery 1. tummychow/git-absorb (~5.8k stars) - a rust port of facebook's hg absorb: stage your review fixes, run it, and it writes a fixup! commit for each hunk, aimed at the commit that should own it. 2. newren/git-filter-repo (~13.5k stars) - a single python script for rewriting a whole repository's history, recommended by the git project over filter-branch and the tool github's docs use for purging files from every commit. 3. arxanas/git-branchless (~4.1k stars) - adds git undo (commits, amends, merges, even rebases), a smartlog view of your commit graph and in-memory rebases to plain git; the readme still labels it alpha. 4. git-town/git-town (~3.4k stars) - a go cli that turns branch chores into commands (hack, sync, propose, ship), with stacked-change helpers like append and prepend and an undo for its own commands. 🖥️ git in your terminal 5. jonas/tig (~13.4k stars) - a text-mode git repository browser written in c, first committed in april 2006, that also stages changes chunk by chunk and doubles as a pager for other git commands. 6. gitui-org/gitui (~22.6k stars) - a keyboard-only terminal ui in rust for staging single hunks or lines, stashing and searching the log; interactive rebase is still on its roadmap to 1.0. 7. so-fancy/diff-so-fancy (~18.1k stars) - a perl script that makes diffs human-readable by stripping the leading +/- markers and simplifying hunk headers; delta even ships an emulation mode for it. 8. dlvhdr/gh-dash (~12.7k stars) - a gh extension that turns pull requests and issues into a keyboard-driven dashboard of sections you define per repo, built on bubble tea and using delta to render pr diffs. 🤝 hooks, changelogs & releases 9. pre-commit/pre-commit (~15.7k stars) - a package manager for git hooks: list them in .pre-commit-config.yaml and it fetches each hook's toolchain without root, even downloading and building node to run eslint. 10. evilmartians/lefthook (~9.0k stars) - a dependency-free go binary from evil martians that runs your git hooks from a lefthook.yml, in parallel, with glob filters and a list of just the staged files for each job. 11. orhun/git-cliff (~12.3k stars) - writes your changelog from git history using conventional commits or regex parsers, with the output shaped by a template and a cliff.toml you control. 12. cli/cli (~46.8k stars) - github's official gh: pull requests, issues and other github concepts in the terminal, right next to your git workflow, and pre-installed on github-hosted runners. 🏗️ closing thoughts some of the best ideas in this issue weren't invented for git. git-absorb ports a facebook mercurial command, jujutsu cites mercurial's revsets and darcs' first-class conflicts as inspirations, and git-branchless goes after an undo that covers a whole repository instead of one ref at a time. git stays the storage layer underneath while the ergonomics arrive from other version control systems, which is a decent argument for reading about ones you'll never use. one warning before you go rewrite everything. a tidy history is a kindness to your reviewers, but rewriting isn't erasing, because clones and forks keep the old commits, so github's docs say to revoke or rotate a leaked secret first. and once you've pushed, treat the history as published. if you must rewrite a shared branch, use --force-with-lease, which fails when the remote branch isn't where you last saw it, and tell your team before you press enter. which git command do you still refuse to touch without a backup branch? tell me on x (twitter) or linkedin. until next thursday, keep your servers close and support your local maintainers.

title: NIGHT_OF_THE_LIVING_FORKS
description: Open-source projects the community raised from the dead after license changes and corporate takeovers—featuring Valkey, OpenTofu, and OpenBao.
content: 🗞️ issue 011: night of the living forks: open source that refused to stay dead it's halloween week, so let's talk about the undead. every few years, a company that grew up on community contributions decides its open-source license is bad for the quarterly numbers. the playbook barely changes: a blog post about the "evolution" of the licensing model, a new license file with words like "source available" or "business source", and a polite note that the code is still open—just not for your cloud provider, your competitor, or anyone who runs it as a service. elastic did it in 2021. lightbend did it to akka in 2022. hashicorp did it to terraform and vault in 2023. redis did it in 2024. here's the part the boardroom keeps forgetting: you can't un-release code. every version already published under an open license stays open forever, and a community with a git clone and a grudge can pick it up the next morning. this week is about the projects that clawed their way back out of the grave—forks that didn't just survive the funeral, but kept shipping releases long after the eulogies were written. grab your coffee. open your terminal. let's start hacking. 🔬 the sandbox: 3 projects i tested this week 1. valkey 🧛 (in-memory data store) what is it? valkey is a high-performance key-value data store forked from redis 7.2.4 in march 2024, right before redis switched to source-available licenses. it lives under the linux foundation with a bsd 3-clause license, it was backed by aws, google and oracle from day one, and it just shipped version 9.1.3. why you should care: valkey speaks the same resp protocol and the same commands, and it still answers info with redis_version:7.2.4, so redis-py, ioredis, jedis and every other client library keep working without a single code change. if redis 7.2 or earlier is your cache, session store or job queue, swapping the binary is the cheapest license insurance you'll ever buy. redis 7.4 and later write data files valkey can't read, so those need a migration rather than a swap. my rating: undead throughput 4.8/5 ⭐ website: github.com/valkey-io/valkey 💻 get started: brew install valkey && valkey-server --daemonize yes && valkey-cli ping 2. opentofu 🧟 (infrastructure as code) what is it? opentofu is the community fork of terraform, started in august 2023 after hashicorp moved terraform 1.6 and later to the business source license. it's a linux foundation project under mpl 2.0 that runs your existing .tf files, modules and providers, and it has since shipped features terraform users had been asking for for years, like client-side state encryption. why you should care: your infrastructure code is the last thing you want held hostage by a license change. for most projects, migrating means installing tofu and running tofu init inside your existing terraform directory—no rewrite, no new language, and the plan you get should look exactly like the one you had yesterday. my rating: drop-in necromancy 4.9/5 ⭐ website: github.com/opentofu/opentofu 💻 get started: brew install opentofu && tofu init && tofu plan 3. openbao 👻 (secrets management) what is it? openbao is the community fork of hashicorp vault, built from the last mpl-licensed code after vault 1.15 and later moved to the business source license. it stores and hands out secrets, certificates and encryption keys behind policies and audit logs, it's developed under the linux foundation umbrella, and its cli is simply called bao. why you should care: secrets management is the worst possible place for a license surprise: it sits in every deploy pipeline, every ci job and every service's startup path. openbao keeps the vault model you already know—the kv engine, policies, the same /v1/ api paths—under mpl 2.0, and bao server -dev gives you an unsealed, in-memory server for local testing in one command. my rating: ghost in the keychain 4.6/5 ⭐ website: github.com/openbao/openbao 💻 get started: brew install openbao && bao server -dev ☕ the curious non-dev: no code required if a company owns the code, how can anyone fork it and keep it free? an open-source license is a promise attached to a specific version of the code. when a company changes its license, it can only change the terms for future versions—everything it already published under the old open license stays open forever. a fork is simply a group of people taking that last open version, giving it a new name (the trademark stays with the company), and continuing the work from there. think of a recipe printed in a cookbook: the publisher can stop printing new editions, but it can't take back the copies already sitting on everyone's shelves. the surprising part is how often the forks win. the companies that depend on a project—cloud providers, linux distributions, banks—usually prefer one run by a neutral foundation, so they move their engineers and their money to the fork. and that pressure works: elastic added the open-source agpl license back to elasticsearch in 2024, and redis did the same in 2025. 📡 the radar: 12 more forks to raise this weekend 🦇 escaped from oracle's crypt 1. mariadb/server (~8.5k stars) - monty widenius's fork of mysql, started in 2009 as oracle moved to buy sun, and now the mysql-compatible server most linux distributions ship by default. 2. libreoffice/core (~4.6k stars) - the document foundation's 2010 fork of openoffice.org, created when most of the community walked away from oracle; the office suite nearly every linux desktop ships today. 3. jenkinsci/jenkins (~26.7k stars) - hudson's community renamed the project jenkins in 2011 after a trademark dispute with oracle, and the fork became one of the most widely deployed ci servers on the planet. 4. illumos/illumos-gate (~1.9k stars) - the opensolaris kernel and core userland, kept alive after oracle shut opensolaris down in 2010; it still powers omnios, smartos and openindiana. 🧛 the relicensing undead 5. opensearch-project/opensearch (~13.9k stars) - aws's 2021 fork of elasticsearch 7.10 after elastic dropped apache 2.0, now governed by the opensearch software foundation under the linux foundation. 6. apache/pekko (~1.7k stars) - the apache software foundation's fork of akka 2.6, taken just before akka adopted the business source license; actors, streams and clustering for java and scala. 7. lxc/incus (~6.5k stars) - the linux containers community's fork of lxd after canonical took the project in-house in 2023, maintained by the same team that first created lxd; system containers and vms from one cli. 8. openvoxproject/openvox (~0.2k stars) - the vox pupuli community's build of puppet, started in late 2024 after perforce stopped publishing public open-source packages; effectively the same as puppet, so existing manifests and modules keep working. 🧟 community coups 9. neovim/neovim (~103k stars) - started in 2014 to refactor vim for async jobs, embedding and lua plugins; the fork has since passed 100,000 github stars. 10. jellyfin/jellyfin (~58.7k stars) - forked from emby in 2018 after emby went closed source; a free media server with no premium tier and no account required. 11. nextcloud/server (~37.3k stars) - forked from owncloud in 2016 by its founder and core developers; self-hosted files, calendar, contacts and office under the agpl. 12. forgejo/forgejo (~5.7k stars) - a community fork of gitea started in 2022 after gitea's domain and trademark moved to a for-profit company; a lightweight self-hosted git forge with built-in actions ci, hosted on codeberg. 🏗️ closing thoughts the license changes of the past five years were sold as protection against cloud giants freeloading on open source. in practice, the cloud giants were among the first to fund the forks—aws built opensearch, and aws, google and oracle lined up behind valkey within days. the people left stranded were the volunteer contributors whose patches suddenly shipped under terms they never agreed to. that's why the most important line in a project's readme isn't the star count; it's who owns the copyright and whether contributors sign a cla that lets one company relicense their work. a project governed by a neutral foundation can't be relicensed over a weekend. and the dead do come back, eventually: hashicorp's own license turns every terraform release back into mpl 2.0 four years after it ships, which means terraform 1.6.0 rises from the grave in october 2027. until then, the forks are doing the work—so send them a bug report, a sponsorship, or at least a star. have you migrated something from redis, terraform or vault to a fork—or decided to stay put? tell me how it went on x (twitter) or linkedin. until next thursday, keep your servers close and support your local maintainers.

title: THE_CVE_SEASON
description: Auditing, patching, and zero-day hunting straight from your terminal—featuring Trivy, Nuclei, and Google's OSV-Scanner.
content: 🗞️ issue 010: cve season: auditing, patching, and zero-day hunting your package-lock.json, go.sum, and base alpine images are crime scenes waiting for a disclosure embargo to lift. every week brings another memory corruption bug in a core c library, a malicious transitive dependency slipped into a package registry, or an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw in an ingress controller you deployed two years ago and forgot about. treating security auditing as a quarterly compliance checkbox—or worse, muting automated pull requests until friday afternoon—is no longer viable when automated exploit scanners start sweeping public ip ranges within fifteen minutes of a public patch commit. survival in modern systems engineering means shifting vulnerability verification and supply chain auditing straight into your local terminal and pre-commit hooks. you don't need another seven-figure enterprise dashboard that emails pdf reports to management; you need fast, deterministic command-line binaries that inspect container layers, trace actual function reachability in your dependency graph, and run real exploit templates against your local staging environment before you push. grab your coffee. open your terminal. let's start hacking. 🔬 the sandbox: 3 projects i tested this week 1. trivy 🛡️ (container & filesystem vulnerability scanner) what is it? trivy is an all-in-one open-source security scanner that inspects container images, local filesystems, remote git repositories, virtual machine images, and live kubernetes clusters. it detects known os package and language dependency vulnerabilities, infrastructure-as-code (iac) misconfigurations, hardcoded secrets, and software license risks while generating complete software bills of materials (sboms). why you should care: instead of juggling five separate linters for dockerfiles, terraform modules, and language lockfiles, you get a single static go binary that parses everything in seconds locally or in ci without requiring a background daemon or database setup. my rating: swiss-army binary 4.9/5 ⭐ website: github.com/aquasecurity/trivy 💻 get started: brew install trivy && trivy fs --scanners vuln,secret,misconfig . 2. nuclei ⚡ (template-based vulnerability & exploit scanner) what is it? nuclei is a high-performance vulnerability scanner built in go that executes human-readable yaml templates across http, dns, tcp, ssl, websocket, and whois protocols. powered by thousands of community-curated detection rules in nuclei-templates, it simulates real-world exploit requests to verify whether a target is genuinely vulnerable. why you should care: static version matching floods your backlog with false positives, whereas writing or pulling a 20-line yaml template lets you fire the exact payload of a newly disclosed cve against your local service to prove whether your patch actually blocks the exploit. my rating: zero-noise exploit verifier 4.8/5 ⭐ website: github.com/projectdiscovery/nuclei 💻 get started: brew install nuclei && nuclei -u https://localhost:8443 -severity critical,high 3. osv-scanner 🔍 (lockfile & reachability vulnerability auditor) what is it? osv-scanner is google's official go cli frontend to the open-source osv.dev advisory database, built on the extensible osv-scalibr extraction library. it recursively scans 19+ lockfile types, vendored c/c++ source trees, and container layers while offering call-graph analysis and interactive guided remediation. why you should care: it reduces dependency alert fatigue by mapping advisories directly to open, machine-readable package ranges, checking whether your code actually calls the vulnerable function, and calculating which minimal version bump resolves the most cves without breaking your build. my rating: lockfile surgeon 4.7/5 ⭐ website: github.com/google/osv-scanner 💻 get started: brew install osv-scanner && osv-scanner scan source -r . ☕ the curious non-dev: no code required what actually is a cve and cvss score? when a security flaw is discovered in widely used software (like many were this week), the cve program (common vulnerabilities and exposures) assigns it a standardized tracking label—like cve-2026-1234—so engineers worldwide know they are talking about the exact same bug rather than describing it differently in separate bug trackers. think of a cve id as a universal serial number for a specific software defect, while the accompanying cvss (common vulnerability scoring system) score is a 0.0 to 10.0 severity rating calculated from factors like how easy the bug is to trigger over a network and whether it requires a password. here is the catch that trips up non-engineers and executives alike: a "9.8 critical" cvss score measures the theoretical worst-case severity of a flaw in isolation, not the actual risk to your specific product. if a library has a 9.8-rated bug in its image-processing feature, but your application only uses that library to format dates and never touches images, the bug cannot be triggered in your system—which is why smart engineering teams verify reachability before hitting the panic button. 📡 the radar: 12 more projects to spin up this weekend 📦 supply chain & sbom - anchore/grype (~13.1k stars) - scans container images, filesystems, and sbom files for known vulnerabilities across major os distributions and language packages. - anchore/syft (~9.7k stars) - generates detailed software bills of materials (sboms) in cyclonedx and spdx formats from container layers and local directories. - sigstore/cosign (~6.4k stars) - signs, verifies, and attests container images and binaries using keyless ephemeral certificates and transparency logs. - ossf/scorecard (~5.8k stars) - evaluates open-source repositories against automated security heuristics like branch protection, pinned dependencies, and fuzzing coverage. 🔍 static, dynamic & secret scanning (sast / dast) - gitleaks/gitleaks (~30.2k stars) - audits git commit histories, working directories, and staged files at high speed to catch hardcoded api keys, tokens, and private keys. - trufflesecurity/trufflehog (~28.6k stars) - discovers leaked credentials across git repositories, s3 buckets, and filesystems while actively verifying whether each key is still live. - semgrep/semgrep (~17.2k stars) - runs syntax-aware static code analysis across 30+ languages using pattern rules that look like actual source code instead of complex regexes. - zaproxy/zaproxy (~16.0k stars) - intercepts, fuzzes, and actively probes web applications and apis for injection flaws and broken authentication during local testing or ci runs. 🛡️ runtime, container & infrastructure auditing - cisofy/lynis (~16.5k stars) - performs deep local security audits, kernel parameter checks, and system hardening assessments directly on linux, macos, and bsd hosts. - prowler-cloud/prowler (~15.1k stars) - executes hundreds of security posture and compliance checks across aws, azure, gcp, and kubernetes environments straight from the cli. - kubescape/kubescape (~11.8k stars) - audits kubernetes manifests, helm charts, and live clusters against nsa-cisa and mitre att&ck frameworks while supporting automated image patching. - falcosecurity/falco (~9.5k stars) - monitors linux kernel syscalls and container runtime activity via ebpf to alert on shell spawns, unexpected file reads, and privilege escalations in real time. 🏗️ closing thoughts security isn't a state you achieve once your ci pipeline turns green; it's a continuous tax you pay for building on top of millions of lines of other people's code. every dependency you add to save twenty minutes of coding today is a codebase you implicitly volunteered to audit, upgrade, and patch for the rest of your system's lifespan. the goal of running these scanners locally isn't to reach some mythical zero-vulnerability utopia—it's to know exactly what is inside your binaries so you can separate real, reachable exploit paths from background noise. and when a critical cve does drop in an upstream library you rely on, remember that the person cutting the patch at 2:00 am is often an unpaid volunteer maintaining critical infrastructure in their spare time. audit your own stack ruthlessly, trim the dependencies you don't need, and treat upstream maintainers like the human beings keeping our industry afloat. i'd love to hear what cli tools or pre-commit workflows you swear by to cut down on dependency noise—reach out on x (twitter) or linkedin and let me know! until next thursday, keep your servers close and support your local maintainers.

title: THE_DECOMPILATION_ENGINES
description: How AI-assisted decompilation engines are turning stripped assembly into readable code—featuring Cutter, OSS-Fuzz, and Ghidra.
content: 🗞️ issue 009: the decompilation engines reverse engineering used to take 40 hours of staring at ida pro assembly and hex dumps. now, the foundational open-source tools we rely on are evolving, acting as vehicles for local decompilation engines, turning stripped assembly back into readable c, discovering hidden apis, and mapping closed binary protocols in minutes. we are shifting from manual static analysis to semantic inference. it is no longer just about reading instruction sets; it is about letting these massive frameworks infer the original developer's intent from the compiled rubble. grab your coffee. open your terminal. let's start hacking. 🔬 the sandbox: 3 projects i tested this week 1. cutter ✂️ (reverse engineering platform) what is it? cutter is a free and open-source reverse engineering platform powered by rizin. it is written in c++ and supports both python and native c++ plugins across linux, macos, and windows. why you should care: it provides advanced debugging, binary analysis, and decompilation using an integrated ghidra decompiler plugin (rz-ghidra). cutter serves as a powerful gui baseline for malware analysis and is increasingly acting as the host platform for community-driven ai analysis plugins. my rating: the cleanest gui 4.5/5 ⭐ website: github.com/rizinorg/cutter brew install --cask cutter 2. oss-fuzz 👾 (continuous fuzzing) what is it? google's continuous fuzzing framework—paired with cifuzz and clusterfuzzlite for github actions ci workflows—that automatically tests c, c++, rust, go, java/jvm, python, javascript, and lua projects for vulnerabilities. why you should care: it finds memory corruption and logic bugs before they hit production, and google has integrated llms (via oss-fuzz-gen) to automatically generate fuzz targets. this ai-powered harness generation discovered 30 new bugs across major projects like openssl (cve-2024-9143) and sqlite3 that were completely unreachable by existing human-written harnesses. my rating: infrastructure standard 5/5 ⭐ website: github.com/google/oss-fuzz git clone https://github.com/google/oss-fuzz.git && cd oss-fuzz && python3 infra/helper.py build_image zlib 3. ghidra 🐉 (sre framework) what is it? a free and open-source software reverse engineering (sre) framework created and maintained by the national security agency (nsa) research directorate. it is written in java with a c++ decompiler component. why you should care: since its public release in 2019, ghidra has become the definitive open-source alternative to proprietary tools like ida pro. its headless mode and extensible java-based extension framework form the absolute backbone for almost all modern ai-assisted decompilation scripts and pipelines. my rating: the ultimate default 5/5 ⭐ website: github.com/nationalsecurityagency/ghidra brew install --cask --no-quarantine ghidra ☕ the curious non-dev: no code required what actually happens during decompilation? when compiling languages like c++, human context such as variable names, function names, and structural logic is stripped away into raw machine code. traditional reverse engineering relies on decompilers to guess this lost structure using rigid, programmed rules. llms transform this process through pattern recognition. trained on millions of paired open-source functions and assembly outputs, specialized models can infer the programmer's intent. instead of translating operations literally, an ai recognizes higher-level patterns, reconstructs clean source code, and contextually restores intuitive names for missing variables. 📡 the radar: 12 more projects to spin up this weekend 🛠️ the framework integrations - justicerage/gepetto (~3.5k stars) - an ida pro python plugin that queries models like openai, anthropic, or local ollama instances to explain decompiled functions and automatically rename variables. - symgraph/ghidrassist (~750 stars) - an llm-powered official ai integration for the radare2 framework, allowing local llms (via ollama or llama.cpp) and cloud models to interact directly with your console in agentic react mode. - wader/fq (~10.6k stars) - not strictly ai, but the ultimate jq for binary formats—essential for parsing undocumented structures before feeding them to models. 🐛 fuzzing & protocol analysis - google/oss-fuzz-gen (~1.4k stars) - the llm-powered sub-framework that generates and benchmarks ai fuzz targets for real-world projects via the oss-fuzz platform. - aflplusplus/aflplusplus (~6.8k stars) - the standard fuzzer; exploration loops. - mandiant/capa (~6.2k stars) - identifies capabilities in executable files; frequently wrapped with ai to explain the detected rule matches. 🧠 symbolic execution & analysis - angr/angr (~9.2k stars) - the premier binary analysis framework; researchers are now piping angr's symbolic states into llms for vulnerability discovery. - jonathansalwan/triton (~4.3k stars) - a dynamic binary analysis and symbolic execution library (an actively maintained alternative to trail of bits' archived trailofbits/manticore at ~3.9k stars), ideal for ai-assisted deobfuscation and state exploration. - albertan017/llm4decompile (~7.1k stars) - open-source models specifically fine-tuned for treating x86_64 disassembly-to-c decompilation and ghidra pseudo-code refinement as a neural translation task. - ev-flow/quark-engine (~1.7k stars) - an android malware scoring system utilizing dalvik bytecode analysis, now shipping built-in ai skills for automated apk analysis and rule generation. 🏗️ closing thoughts ai isn't replacing the reverse engineer anytime soon, as it still hallucinates apis and botches complex pointer arithmetic. but it has fundamentally lowered the activation energy required to map out a hostile binary. the grunt work of renaming a thousand stripped functions is largely solved, freeing you up to focus on the actual vulnerability research and system architecture using heavyweights like ghidra and cutter. test these frameworks and their llm plugins against some old crackmes or malware samples this weekend. you will be surprised at how fast title: THE_OPEN_SOURCE_ENTERPRISE
description: The open-source rebellion against enterprise software—from personal wealth OS platforms to fully decoupled business intelligence.
content: 🗞️ issue 008: the open-source enterprise the enterprise software market has been broken for a long time. founders, economists, and analysts are locked into massive, bloated saas subscriptions just to parse their own data or manage their own balance sheets. we normally spend thursdays hacking in the it world, but this week, we are stepping into the boardrooms and exploring the open-source rebellion against enterprise software—from personal wealth os platforms to fully decoupled business intelligence. grab your coffee. open your terminal. let's start hacking business. 🔬 the sandbox: 3 projects i tested this week 1. maybe 💰 (finance os) what is it? a wildly popular, beautifully designed open-source operating system for wealth management and personal/business finance. it gives you full ownership over your financial data. why you should care: financial aggregators make their money by selling your transactional data to third parties. "maybe" allows you to self-host a completely private, localized dashboard to track your net worth, run financial projections, and categorize spending without handing your banking data to a marketing firm. my rating: absolute game changer 5/5 ⭐ website: github.com/maybe-finance/maybe 💻 get started: docker run -d -p 3000:3000 -e secret_key_base=your_secret_key maybeapp/maybe:latest note: it's no longer actively developed! 2. metabase 📊 (business intelligence) what is it? an incredibly powerful open-source business intelligence server that plugs directly into any database (postgresql, mysql, snowflake) and lets anyone visualize data instantly without writing a single line of sql. why you should care: companies large sums on enterprise bi tools, locking their analysts into proprietary ecosystems. metabase allows economists and data analysts to spin up complex interactive dashboards and internal reporting tools entirely on open-source infrastructure. and personalise it for their own needs. my rating: essential infrastructure 5/5 ⭐ website: github.com/metabase/metabase 💻 get started: docker run -d -p 3000:3000 --name metabase metabase/metabase 3. erpnext 🏭 (enterprise resource planning) what is it? a monolithic, open-source enterprise resource planning (erp) system built by frappe. it comes loaded with modules for accounting, hr, manufacturing, crm, and inventory management. why you should care: erp software is the backbone of the physical economy, but the market is heavily monopolized by legacy giants like sap and oracle who charge exorbitant licensing fees. erpnext proves that a modern, open-source framework can actually run the financial and logistical operations of a massive enterprise securely and for free. my rating: flawless execution 5/5 ⭐ website: github.com/frappe/erpnext 💻 get started: docker run -d -p 8080:8080 frappe/erpnext ☕ the curious non-dev: no code required what is open-source enterprise software? "open-source enterprise" defies this. the source code for massive tools is published for free on the internet. a company can download the code, install it on their own private servers (self-hosting), and use it forever without paying a subscription. this gives businesses ultimate data privacy, total customization, and zero risk of the software company suddenly doubling their prices. 📡 the radar: 12 more projects to spin up this weekend 💼 financial infrastructure & accounting - title: THE_MOBILE_DEV_BLUEPRINT
description: The mobile dev ecosystem is finally maturing. A look at Scrcpy, Expo, and Google's Now in Android.
content: 🗞️ issue 007: the mobile dev blueprint the mobile development landscape is notoriously fragmented. for the past decade, developers have fought a holy war between writing pure native code for ios and android, or relying on cross-platform frameworks to bridge the gap. but over the last few years, the tooling has matured to a point where you no longer have to sacrifice performance for convenience. in this week's issue, we are diving deep into the mobile ecosystem. we’re covering aggressive android hardware mirroring, the undisputed king of cross-platform react frameworks, and the absolute gold standard for modern native kotlin architecture. grab your coffee. open your terminal. let's start hacking. 🔬 the sandbox: 3 projects i tested this week 1. scrcpy 📱 (hardware control) what is it? a lightweight, insanely fast c application that allows you to mirror and completely control your android device from your computer via usb or tcp/ip. it requires absolutely no root access and no app installation on the phone. why you should care: if you build mobile apps, testing gestures and typing on a physical device while glued to your ide is a nightmare. scrcpy routes your desktop keyboard, mouse, and even audio directly to the physical device with near-zero latency, turning your physical phone into a seamless window on your mac. my rating: flawless execution 5/5 ⭐ website: github.com/genymobile/scrcpy 💻 get started: brew install scrcpy android-platform-tools 2. expo ⚛️ (cross-platform framework) what is it? the ultimate open-source framework for building native applications on ios, android, and the web from a single javascript/typescript codebase. why you should care: setting up xcode and android studio to compile react native is historically brutal. expo abstracts away the complex native build pipelines, provides a massive standard library of native apis (camera, file system, haptics), and lets you push over-the-air updates to your users without going through the app store review process. my rating: absolute game changer 5/5 ⭐ website: github.com/expo/expo 💻 get started: npx create-expo-app@latest my-app 3. now in android 🤖 (native architecture) what is it? google's official, fully functional reference application built entirely with kotlin and jetpack compose. it is actively maintained by the android engineering team to showcase best practices. why you should care: the android development ecosystem moves fast, and old tutorials become deprecated quickly. whenever you find yourself asking, "what is the correct, modern way to handle state, dependency injection, or navigation in android right now?"—this repo is the living, breathing answer. my rating: essential reference 5/5 ⭐ website: github.com/android/nowinandroid 💻 get started: git clone https://github.com/android/nowinandroid.git ☕ the curious non-dev: no code required what is cross-platform vs. native development? if you want to build an app for both iphones and androids, you traditionally had to hire two different teams. one team would write swift code for ios (native), and another team would write kotlin code for android (native). this is potentially expensive and slow. frameworks like react native (and expo) or flutter solved this by allowing developers to write their code once in javascript or dart. when the app is compiled, the framework acts like an interpreter—it translates that single javascript codebase into the native ui components that both apple and google expect. you get two apps "for the price of one" without sacrificing the native feel in some cases. 📡 the radar: 12 more projects to spin up this weekend 🏗️ the titans (massive ecosystems) - flutter (179k+ stars) - google's juggernaut framework for building natively compiled applications from a single codebase. - ignite (19.9k+ stars) - infinite red's battle-tested react native boilerplate, cli, and component generator. - tamagui (14k+ stars) - an insanely fast universal ui kit and optimizing compiler that gives 100% style parity between react native and the web. - colima (30k+ stars) - container runtimes on macos with minimal setup (a massive favorite for ios/rn devs replacing docker desktop). ⚡ react native power-ups - ui kitten (10k+ stars) - a massive, highly customizable react native ui library based on the eva design system. - vision camera (9.6k+ stars) - the absolute undisputed king of high-performance camera libraries in react native, built by margelo. - flash-list (7.2k+ stars) - built by shopify, this is a drop-in replacement for flatlist that renders instantly and solves rn's massive scrolling performance issues. - radon ide (1.7k+ stars) - a brand new vscode/cursor extension from software mansion that turns your standard editor into a full-featured ide specifically for react native and expo. 🛠️ system design & utilities - mobile system design (5.8k+ stars) - an insanely popular open-source framework and guide for passing mobile system design interviews. - docker-android (15.8k+ stars) - a complete android emulator running inside a docker container (perfect for ci/cd testing). - android-databackup (7.3k+ stars) - a modern, open-source titanium-backup alternative for root users. - atoll (4.7k+ stars) - an open-source project that perfectly recreates the ios "dynamic island" natively on macos. 🏗️ closing thoughts mobile development has evolved from a fragmented mess of clunky emulators and deprecated libraries into a streamlined, high-performance ecosystem. whether you are hacking hardware layers with scrcpy, pushing over-the-air updates with expo, or building reference-grade native apps, the open-source community is building the exact tools you need to ship faster. i'd love to hear what incredible mobile projects
